title: Help these women (Philippians 4:1–3)
hookLine: Euodia and Syntyche, co-workers, are asked to agree

cards: Two names, and that's almost all we know: Euodia and Syntyche. Paul's letter will be read aloud to the whole church at Philippi, and in the middle of it he names two women who aren't getting along.
We don't know what the quarrel was about. Money, a meeting, a hurt word, a plan for the church. The letter never says, and it's honest to leave it there.
What we do know is how Paul handles it. He doesn't take a side. He doesn't send a rebuke.

teach.b: First he speaks to the whole church with real warmth: they are, in the King James Bible, "my joy and crown."

teach.h: BESEECH, AND BESEECH: NO SIDE TAKEN.
teach.b: Then: "I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord." He says beseech twice, once to each woman. Neither is named first as the problem.
And same mind is a phrase from all through this letter: be likeminded, let this mind be in you. It doesn't mean agreeing on every detail. It means facing the same direction.
Then he turns to someone else: "And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel." Who is the yokefellow? Nobody knows.
Some think it's a friend Paul doesn't name. Some think Syzygos, Greek for yokefellow, was the man's actual name. Either way, a third person is asked to help two people find their way back.

teach.h: CO-WORKERS, NAMES IN THE BOOK OF LIFE.
teach.b: And look how Paul describes these women: not as troublemakers, but as co-workers who labored with him in the gospel, along with Clement and the rest, "whose names are in the book of life."

teach.h: BE OF THE SAME MIND IN THE LORD.
teach.b: Their quarrel doesn't cancel their work. Philippi's church began, Acts says, with women at a place of prayer by a river, and Lydia opening her home. Women were there from the start.
This week has walked through Philippians: look to others, he emptied himself, shine like stars, two helpers honored, counting it loss, press on, and now two co-workers asked to agree.

how: Many churches ask a trusted third person, a pastor, elder or friend, to help members reconcile, and some read Philippians 4:2–3 when teaching about peacemaking in the congregation.

o: a deacon who carried Paul's letters to Philippi
yokefellow: one who pulls in the same yoke
a judge called in to settle a church quarrel

games.q: what's inside Philippians 4:1–3 — tap the pairs.
p: asked to be of the same mind

s: the letter tells us what the two women argued about
it never says. we only know Paul asked them to agree.
Paul calls the two women his co-workers in the gospel
he says they labored with him, along with Clement and others.
Paul names one of the women as the one to blame
he says beseech twice, once to each, and takes no side.

games.q: you're Paul. two of your co-workers in a church you love have fallen out. the letter will be read aloud to everyone. what do you do?
o: tell the church which one is right.
plead with both equally and ask a friend to help them.
leave it out of the letter.
games.why: he beseeches each by name, then asks a "true yokefellow" to help them. no side taken, and their work honored.

practice: Think of two people you know who have drifted apart or fallen out, friends, siblings, coworkers, and don't decide who's right; Paul didn't.

Picture each of them and remember one good thing each has done, then ask whether there's a small way to help without taking sides, even just by not feeding the quarrel. If you pray, you can hold both of them before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Syzygos. Greek for yokefellow, one who pulls in the same yoke, maybe even the man's own name: Paul's friend, asked to help Euodia and Syntyche find the same mind again.

orig.note: Greek: yokefellow, one who pulls in the same yoke. some think it was the man's actual name.

carryVoice: Your line: be of one mind. Facing the same direction, not agreeing on everything. A week of Philippians, done.
